summary: The SHAPE is right and I am not filing against it: nothing in production pipelines -- CommitLog.commit() is a synchronous putIfAbsent-fold-retry loop -- so an ordering guard in the write path would guard nothing, would be invented structure, and would widen the row. Keeping checkAckOrder out of checkChain is also right: checkChain's input is a store, and a store cannot supply an ack order. The javadoc states the by-accident consequence rather than hiding it. What is wrong is the TYPE the right shape was built on. AckEvent carries a bare sequence and no chain identity, and the scan runs `for (long lower = 0; lower < e.sequence(); lower++)`, so the checker reads I5's 'every lower-numbered write IN THE CHAIN' as 'every non-negative long below this sequence, anywhere in the trace'. Sequence numbers restart at 0 per epoch -- ChainReplay.java:392, 'OFFSETS CROSS, SEQUENCE NUMBERS DO NOT' -- and M4.13, the row's own named consumer, is the failover simulation. MEASURED in a copy of the staged bytes: a two-chain trace where the second writer acks its sequence 2 having confirmed nothing of its own chain returns ZERO violations; a strictly serial single-chain trace beginning at sequence 1000 returns FOUR. Wrong in both directions, and neither precondition is written down. Separately MEASURED: restricting the scan to the immediately-lower sequence -- `for (long lower = Math.max(0, e.sequence() - 1); ...)` -- passes all six tests in AckOrderTest, so the suite constrains 'the adjacent write was confirmed', not 'every lower-numbered write'. ADR-0011's own scenario is three concurrent writes (N+1, N+2, N+3), and no trace in the suite has pipeline depth above two. Cost lens: checkAckOrder issues no get/put/list/stat and adds no object-store request of any kind; the request rate is unchanged by this diff. Its CPU cost is filed as a minor with numbers.

findings.title: checkAckOrder drops the chain I5 is scoped to: false negative across a failover, false positive on any trace not beginning at sequence 0
findings.detail: I5's clause is 'every lower-numbered write IN THE CHAIN has been confirmed'. AckEvent is `record AckEvent(long sequence, boolean isAck)` -- no epoch, no chain id -- and the scan is `for (long lower = 0; lower < e.sequence(); lower++)` against a single `confirmed` HashSet spanning the whole trace. That substitutes two things for 'the chain': the chain's floor becomes the literal 0, and the chain's extent becomes the trace. Sequence numbers restart at 0 in each epoch's chain (ChainReplay.java:392 states it in as many words: 'OFFSETS CROSS, SEQUENCE NUMBERS DO NOT'; LocalSequencer.java:308-321 opens a fresh CommitLog per minted epoch and recovers it), and the consumer this checker was written for -- M4.13, named in the row and in the javadoc -- is the simulation that injects failovers, so a run's trace spans several chains. MEASURED in a copy of the staged bytes, both directions: (1) FALSE NEGATIVE -- trace [confirmed 0, acked 0, confirmed 1, acked 1, confirmed 2, acked 2, acked 2] read as chain A's three commits followed by chain B acking its own sequence 2 having confirmed NOTHING of chain B, returns 0 violations, because chain A's confirmations satisfy chain B's lookups; (2) FALSE POSITIVE -- a strictly serial, strictly ordered writer whose trace covers sequences 1000..1003 returns 4 violations, one per ack, each reading 'sequence 1000 was ACKED while the lower-numbered write 0 was still unconfirmed'. Neither the record nor the method javadoc states the precondition (single chain, trace begins at sequence 0, no gaps) that would make the implementation correct, and the javadoc paragraph added to the I5 bullet says flatly 'THAT HALF IS NOW CHECKED' in a list whose stated purpose is avoiding exactly that overclaim. The false negative is the damaging one: it is silent, and it hides the one writer the clause exists to catch.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 wires the simulation's per-run ack trace into checkAckOrder, as this row's javadoc says it will. A seed drives a takeover: chain at epoch 4 commits sequences 0..40 correctly, the lease flips, epoch 5 opens a fresh chain, and epoch 5's writer pipelines and acks its sequence 3 while its own sequences 0-2 are still in flight -- the naive pipelining ADR-0011 forbids, on the failover path where a lost CAS against a SEAL is what makes it unsafe. checkAckOrder finds 0, 1 and 2 in `confirmed` -- they are epoch 4's, a different chain, on different keys -- and returns []. The sweep reports the seed clean. The row's entire deliverable is a checker that catches naive pipelining, and it will not catch it in the only place the simulation can produce it. In the other direction, whenever the simulation traces a window of a chain rather than the whole chain from 0, every ack in the window is reported as a violation and a correct writer fails the sweep. Fix is small and stays in the type: give AckEvent an epoch (or chain id) and scope the confirmed set and the lower-bound scan to it, and state the remaining precondition in the javadoc.

findings.title: Surviving mutation: no trace in the suite has pipeline depth above two, so the suite passes a checker that only inspects the adjacent sequence
findings.detail: MEASURED in a copy of the staged bytes: replacing `for (long lower = 0; lower < e.sequence(); lower++)` with `for (long lower = Math.max(0, e.sequence() - 1); lower < e.sequence(); lower++)` -- i.e. check only the immediately-preceding sequence, never 'every lower-numbered write' -- leaves all six AckOrderTest tests GREEN. Every trace in the suite is depth-2: naivePipelined() has two writes, pipelinedButOrderedAcks() has two, and EVERYOutOfOrderAckIsReportedNotJustTheFirst() acks 2 then 1 then 0, where in each case the culprit IS the adjacent sequence. ADR-0011's scenario is stated with three: 'A leader that issues N+1, N+2, N+3 concurrently could have N+2 succeed while N+1 loses to a seal'. The killing trace is one line and is absent: [confirmed 2, confirmed 1, acked 2] -- write 0 still in flight, 1 and 2 landed, 2 acked. MEASURED: the staged code reports 1 violation for it ('sequence 2 was ACKED while the lower-numbered write 0 was still unconfirmed'); the mutant reports 0. This matters more than an ordinary coverage gap because the row's own claim is that the naive pipelining writer was 'written in the test and MEASURED to be caught' -- what was measured is that a depth-2 pipeline is caught, which a much weaker checker also does. Note this is independent of R1a: fixing the chain scoping does not add the depth-3 trace.
findings.failure_scenario: A later change simplifies the scan to the adjacent sequence -- a plausible 'the chain is consecutive, so checking sequence-1 is enough' optimisation, and R1c gives someone a direct incentive to make it, since it turns the O(sequence) loop into O(1). The suite stays green. checkAckOrder then silently accepts precisely the writer ADR-0011 describes: N+2 and N+3 confirmed, N+1 in flight, N+3 acked -- because N+2, its neighbour, is confirmed. The invariant M4.13 is built to enforce reports clean on the failure it was written for.

findings.title: The scan is bounded by the sequence VALUE, not by the trace, so the checker is quadratic in chain length
findings.detail: The inner loop runs from 0 to e.sequence() for every ack, so a clean trace of N commits costs ~N-squared/2 HashSet lookups regardless of how few events the trace holds. MEASURED, warm, in a copy of the staged bytes: N=1,000 acks 6 ms; N=5,000 110 ms; N=10,000 208 ms; N=200,000 75,353 ms. The shape is O(highest sequence) per ack, not O(trace), so a short trace taken late in a long chain pays the full sequence value. The same information is available in O(1) from a watermark -- the lowest sequence not yet confirmed, advanced on each confirmation -- which also removes the incentive named in R1b's failure scenario. Filed as minor, not major, because the budget it threatens belongs to a row that has not landed: M4.24 records the sweep budget as <60s for 1,000 seeds, and at 5,000 commits per seed this checker alone costs 110 s.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 runs its 1,000-seed sweep with the trace wired in. At 5,000 commits per seed the ack check alone spends 110 s against a <60 s budget for the whole sweep, and the obvious remedy under time pressure is either to shorten the runs -- reducing what the sweep examines -- or to make the scan adjacent-only, which R1b MEASURED as invisible to this suite.

findings.title: anEmptyTraceReportsNoVIOLATIONAndNoEVIDENCE asserts only half its own name, and the new entry point reproduces M4.22's CLEAN-vs-UNREAD ambiguity
findings.detail: The test name claims two things -- no violation AND no evidence -- and the body is `assertThat(Invariants.checkAckOrder(List.of())).isEmpty()`, which asserts the first and cannot express the second, since [] is the identical return for a trace that was clean and a trace that was never supplied. That is exactly the defect M4.22 is open for on checkChain ('returns an empty list both for a chain that held nothing wrong and for a chain that was never there ... so a caller cannot tell CLEAN from UNREAD'), now reproduced in a second entry point that M4.22's row does not name.
findings.failure_scenario: M4.13 calls checkAckOrder for a seed whose trace collection was never wired up, or was dropped by a fault-injection path, and gets []. The seed is recorded as upholding I5 when nothing about it was examined. When M4.22 is picked up, its row names checkChain only, so the second entry point is left behind and the ambiguity survives the fix.
